chapters.s: The morning of the announced fast awakened the village's ears before it awakened anything else. The earth on the labourers' footprints had not even dried when the children of the Coconut-Leaf School made their next decision—a one-day screen-fast in Garh Narikel. Ba's spectacles beside the pot, Satyavrat's phone, Devika's device, Meera's thread and the children's register shone together in the moonlight. The screen-fast ended, but its hunger did not.…

The first line written before dawn was now demanding its complete letter. On the second morning after the screen-fast, the village sky seemed a little clearer. The next morning, when children gathered around the stump of Channa Grove, Ananya opened the register and wrote the heading: “Satyavrat's Public Hearing.” Ira placed the letters from distant countries beside it.…

No sooner had that new heading been written in the register than the day of the hearing seemed to stand before them of its own accord. No post office could certify whether Ira’s letter had reached the children abroad. The farther Satyavrat Mehta walked, the more one line written by the children kept sounding in his ears: “Rules are needed to guard names.” He knew that the next day those rules would be asked for a name.…

At dawn that first breath began looking for a body between dry leaves, notebooks, and pens. On the second day after the public hearing, no lesson was taught at the Coconut-Leaf School. The roots of the Channa stump stayed faintly warm all night. The children kept watch in turns. Lamplight trembled over the first page of the constitution, while on the final blank page some invisible hand seemed to wait to write…
chapters.tu: Festive form of the Silent Jhumar

chapters.s: Until the pages of the Constitution of Names dried, a strange peace remained around the cut Channa stump. The rules written by the children—we will not erase names, we will not sell privacy, the body will not be humiliated, no contract upon memory—were descending not only onto paper but onto faces. Ananya wrote the next heading in the register: “The Shade of the Stump.” The black page closed. The stones of names settled in their places. The rogues remained absent, but their shadow became the next day’s lesson.

After the absence of the rogues, the peace that descended upon the village was not the peace of rest but of listening. Even after the assembly ended, people did not rise at once from around the stump. And the water, which until then had been only a smell, was returning.

The farther the stump’s shade spread, the calmer the earth appeared. But the waters of the Kamla-Balan have never trusted silence. The flood had arrived. The names were surviving. Kabaddi had entered the water. And in the grey current of the Kamla-Balan, beyond the shade of the cut Channa tree, the first backs of the crocodiles gleamed again.…

The first testimony that was to rise from beneath the water came on the second night of the flood. That night the water began to reveal its true colour. Thus the return of the crocodiles became not the end of fear, but the beginning of the next struggle. Water had shown the boundary; now greed was coming with papers to purchase even that boundary.
In the final deal, it is not the price that is written—it is the name.

Before the awaited test arrived, a strange calm spread through Garh Narikel after Lau Kin-Hung's final deal. It was not the calm of victory; it held the exhaustion of receding floodwater, the smell of names wet upon stone… At that time no one in Garh Narikel knew this. But the moment Batuknath's belated forgiveness was left incomplete, the next door of the story opened—onto the man who was about to understand that his entire life had itself been a mule account for greed.
The one who made other people's accounts into mules one day woke to find his own life had been a mule account.
The final message cannot be erased—it becomes a leaf and clings to the stump.
The wind tried to carry away the testimony, the water tried to dissolve it—but the testimony was a leaf and did not move.

chapters.t: Elephant, Crocodile, and a Child's Hand
chapters.s: Around the stump and the name-stones, the elephant-crocodile story is retold as a lesson about power, seizure and rescue. The children learn that hearing and carrying a name is a form of liberation, and Chapter 100 closes Part 1 by placing the future of the watch in a child’s hand.
